Risk management

Framework and systems

Risk management is key to the Issuer's operations, to ensuring customer satisfaction and in providing a
stable foundation for generating quality returns for its shareholder. Accordingly, the Issuer has a
comprehensive risk management system supported by an appropriate governance framework and risk
culture that aims to prevent or reduce potential losses.

The Issuer's risk management system has several elements, including a risk management strategy that
outlines its risk appetite; risk management policies and reporting processes implemented in line with
the overall risk strategy; and an ORSA process to evaluate and ensure its solvency on an ongoing basis.

The risk management governance framework has several key stakeholders. The Board of Directors of
the Issuer (the "Board") defines the Issuer's risk appetite and approves the risk management strategy
and policies and the Issuer's overall risk tolerance levels. The Board Risk Committee supports the Board
to develop a suitable risk management system and supervises and provides guidance to ensure its
effective implementation. The Risk Management Division supports the establishment and operation of
an efficient risk management system. The risk management governance framework is complemented
by other committees, such as the Asset - Liability Committee, which is responsible for managing
individual risks.

This risk management system is ultimately supported by an appropriate risk culture, namely a strong
and consistent culture of adhering to regulations, applying sound business practices, and integrating risk
management across all operations and management levels.




                                                  - 129 -

Risk profile

The Issuer continuously evaluates the broader economic environment, ensuring that timely and
appropriate measures are implemented to mitigate emerging risks effectively. The Issuer has identified
a number of major risks to which it may be exposed, which are classified in the following categories:

•       Insurance risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from losses or adverse changes in the
        value of insurance liabilities, due to unsuitable assumptions in pricing and reserving. Exposure
        to insurance risk is mitigated by implementing appropriate underwriting and reserving policies
        and procedures, as well as concluding reinsurance agreements with creditworthy reinsurers.

•       Market risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from fluctuations in the level and in the
        volatility of market prices of assets or liabilities. The Issuer manages market risk by establishing
        limits to ensure a well-diversified investment portfolio, monitoring key risk metrics like 'value
        at risk' to enable prompt corrective actions, and employing hedging strategies when necessary.

•       Credit risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from fluctuations in the credit standing of
        counterparties and debtors to whom the Issuer is exposed or the failure of counterparties and
        debtors to fulfil agreed terms. The Issuer manages credit risk by setting up and regularly
        monitoring time and money limits for the collection of premiums and other receivables and
        entering into transactions with counterparties who fulfil high standards of creditworthiness.

•       Liquidity risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from the inability of the Issuer to fulfil
        its obligations when they become due. The Issuer manages liquidity risk by regularly
        monitoring its cash position and forecasted short-term liquidity needs, setting up and
        monitoring limits to enable prompt corrective actions and maintaining a buffer of high-quality
        liquid assets that can be readily converted into cash at no or very low cost.

•       Operational risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from inadequate or inappropriate
        internal processes, operating systems or human resources or from external factors. The Issuer
        has established an effective operational risk management framework, including appropriate risk
        tolerance limits, to prevent operational risk, where possible, and to detect, assess and manage
        operational risks.

•       Asset-liability mismatch risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from mismatches between
        the Issuer's assets and its liabilities, as well as off-balance sheet items. The mismatch may
        concern the levels and the time structure of the asset and liability cash flows. The Issuer
        manages asset-liability mismatch risk by establishing acceptable mismatch levels and
        monitoring procedures to allow appropriate rebalancing of its investment portfolio.

•       Concentration risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from a significant concentration of
        assets or insurance liabilities in individual items, counterparties or sectors. The Issuer manages
        this risk by aiming to have a diversified insurance portfolio, implementing associated limits in
        its investment portfolio and limiting exposures to other individual counterparties.

•       Sustainability risk: the risk for profits and capital arising from events or circumstances in the
        environmental or social field, or in the Issuer's governance which, if they materialise, could
        have a material adverse effect. The Issuer recognises the significance of sustainability risks and
        is committed to operating in a socially responsible manner, as is evidenced by its overall risk
        appetite statements. It recognises the impact environmental issues can have on its insurance
        portfolio, but also on its operations. It has consequently integrated environmental, social and
        governance ("ESG") aspects into its wider risk management framework, to effectively manage
        relevant exposures.




                                                   - 130 -

•       Other risks: in particular, reputational risk and strategic risk that are managed through cautious
        strategic planning, embedding risk management in its daily operations, the development of a
        sound risk culture and continuous monitoring.

The Issuer's most material quantified risks, as reflected in the composition of its SCR as at 31 December
2025, are market risk (principally driven by movements in credit spreads and fluctuations in the equity
market) and health underwriting risk. The health underwriting risk is primarily associated with a
portfolio of mature hospital products that are no longer actively marketed and are subject to specific
premium adjustment features. Market risk accounts for the largest share of the SCR before
diversification, reflecting the composition and duration profile of the Issuer's investment portfolio.

See "Risk Factors" for further details.

Solvency II Directive

The Issuer is subject to the Solvency II regulatory framework. The Issuer monitors its capital
requirement under Solvency II by examining its SCR and MCR in relation to solvency boundaries set
internally and externally by European and national regulatory frameworks.

Through its capital management, the Issuer aims to optimise the balance between risk and return while
properly ensuring its capital adequacy. The Issuer's Capital Management Policy establishes capital
adequacy limits on the Solvency II ratio, specifying actions that may be taken to restore the ratio to
desired levels. As at the date of this Offering Circular, the SCR is monitored monthly using
approximation methods, with a full analytical calculation performed quarterly and submitted to the BoG
on a private basis.

To determine capital adequacy, the Issuer assesses the classification of own funds by examining
whether they meet the supervisory framework criteria for each tier of own funds and by applying the
relevant quantitative limits for eligibility. Its risk management procedures measure risks by taking into
account the relevant provisions of Solvency II.

Regulatory Framework - EU and Greek regulations

Solvency II framework

The EU insurance framework establishes risk-based capital and solvency requirements principally
under the Solvency II Directive. Implementing measures are set out in Commission Delegated
Regulation (EU) 2015/35, as amended, which is directly applicable in each Member State. The main
aim of the Solvency II framework is to ensure the financial stability of the insurance industry across the
EU and to protect policyholders by establishing solvency requirements better matched to the true risks
of the business. The Solvency II framework adopts a three-pillar approach: (i) quantitative requirements
(Pillar 1), including requirements to hold own funds equal to or in excess of an SCR and an MCR; (ii)
qualitative requirements (Pillar 2), covering effective governance systems proportionate to the business,
risk management functions, internal controls, actuarial functions, compliance functions, ORSA and
control over outsourcing arrangements; and (iii) supervisory reporting and public disclosure
requirements (Pillar 3). Under the Solvency II framework, basic own funds are derived from the
solvency balance sheet in which assets and liabilities are valued on an economic basis, and are
categorised into three tiers with differing qualifications as eligible regulatory capital. Moreover, a single
passport principle applies whereby a licence from a competent authority in a Member State is valid
throughout the EEA.

Greek Law 4364/2016, as amended and in force, transposed Solvency II Directive into Greek law (the
"Greek Insurance Regulation Law"). The Greek Insurance Regulation Law has been in force since 1
January 2016 and governs the taking-up and pursuit of direct insurance and reinsurance activities in
Greece, the supervision of insurance and reinsurance groups, and the reorganisation and winding-up of
insurance undertakings. It sets forth capital adequacy and solvency requirements, defines classes of
insurance business, and establishes the framework for the corporate governance of insurance
undertakings. It also establishes the framework for the special liquidation of insurers, including licence
revocation, the appointment of an insurance liquidator and the ranking of claims against an insolvent
insurer.

Bank of Greece prudential supervision

Under the Greek Insurance Regulation Law, the BoG is the competent supervisory authority for the
insurance sector in Greece.

The BoG exercises prudential supervision of Greek insurance undertakings through its Occupational
and Private Insurance Supervision Directorate. As the competent supervisory authority, the BoG is
responsible for: (i) granting and revoking the authorisations of insurance and reinsurance undertakings,
including the expansion into additional classes of the insurance business; (ii) ongoing prudential



                                                   - 135 -

supervision of insurance undertakings, including monitoring compliance with the requirements of
Solvency II in respect of capital adequacy, systems of governance, risk management and regulatory
reporting; (iii) monitoring compliance with applicable Greek and EU legislation, including conduct-of-
business rules and obligations relating to the prevention of money laundering and the countering of the
financing of terrorism; and (iv) imposing administrative measures and sanctions where infringements
are identified. In addition, the BoG cooperates with EIOPA, and with the competent supervisory
authorities of other EU Member States, in the context of cross-border business or the provision of
services under the freedom to provide services.

The regular and effective supervision exercised by the BoG over the solvency of insurance and
reinsurance undertakings is based on a comprehensive framework of reporting obligations imposed on
the supervised entities. In this context, undertakings are required to submit to the BoG, inter alia, an
annual solvency and financial condition report; a regular supervisory report; an ORSA supervisory
report; and quantitative supervisory reports on their basic own funds, the SCR and the MCR on both a
quarterly and annual basis with varying levels of detail, in accordance with the Solvency II reporting
framework. These documents are submitted to the BoG on a private and confidential basis, other than
the annual solvency and financial condition report, which is published. Furthermore, insurance and
reinsurance undertakings may be subject to additional regular or ad-hoc reporting requirements
depending on their business activities and the covered classes of insurance they underwrite.

The BoG has supervisory power to take preventive and corrective measures where it identifies risks to
the solvency position, financial condition, governance standards or risk profile of an insurance
undertaking. Such measures may include requiring the undertaking to strengthen its own funds,
restricting or prohibiting certain business activities, requiring changes to the undertaking's risk profile
or governance arrangements, restricting the free disposal of assets and, where applicable, restricting
distributions or payments on own funds items.

Qualifying holdings and fit and proper supervision

Acquisitions or disposals of a 'qualifying holding' (i.e. a direct or indirect holding of at least 10 per cent.
of share capital or voting rights, or any other possibility of exercising significant influence over
management) require prior BoG approval under Article 43 of the Greek Insurance Regulation Law. It
is also necessary to obtain the approval of the BoG for any subsequent acquisition of shares in an
insurance company exceeding (or which may result in the total holding of the same person to exceed)
one-fifth, one-third or half of the share capital or voting rights in, or the acquisition of direct or indirect
control of, the insurance company. The BoG assesses the proposed acquirer evaluating, inter alia, the
suitability ('fit and proper' test) of the proposed acquirer, financial soundness, transparency of the
corporate/group structure, money laundering and terrorist financing risks, and the implications for the
solvency and governance system of the insurance undertaking.

Senior managers and board members of insurance undertakings must satisfy fit and proper requirements
under Article 31 of the Greek Insurance Regulation Law, demonstrating adequate skills, knowledge,
and experience commensurate to the size, nature and complexity of the undertaking's operations, as
well as good reputation and integrity. Insurance undertakings are required to maintain procedures for
(i) the pre-selection, assessment and approval of new board members and key function holders, (ii) the
ongoing fit and proper assessment of such persons, and (iii) immediate notification to the supervisory
authority in case of changes or identified deficiencies in the suitability of such persons.

Capital adequacy supervision

The Solvency II framework, as transposed by the Greek Insurance Regulation Law, establishes a
graduated supervisory response to capital adequacy deterioration. Where the Issuer's eligible own funds
fall below the SCR, the BoG must be notified immediately under Article 109 of the Greek Insurance
Regulation Law. The Issuer must then, within two months, submit a realistic recovery plan to restore



                                                    - 136 -

coverage of the SCR within six months (extendable by up to three months in exceptional
circumstances). During the period of non-compliance and in exceptional circumstances, the BoG may
restrict or prohibit free disposal of the Issuer's assets and may restrict or prohibit distributions on own
funds items, including, where applicable, payments on certain regulatory capital instruments (including
the Notes).

A breach of the MCR triggers a more severe supervisory response. Under Article 110 of the Greek
Insurance Regulation Law, the Issuer must immediately notify the BoG and, within one month, submit
a short-term finance scheme. The BoG may restrict or prohibit free disposal of assets and, if it considers
that the Issuer's financial position will deteriorate further, may take all measures necessary to safeguard
policyholder interests, including restricting or suspending distributions on own funds instruments (such
as the Notes). Failure to restore compliance with the MCR within the statutory period may lead to
withdrawal of the Issuer's licence and the commencement of special liquidation under Articles 235 to
248 of the Greek Insurance Regulation Law. If special liquidation proceedings were commenced in
respect of the Issuer, claims against the Issuer would be treated in accordance with the mandatory
creditor hierarchy applicable to Greek insurance undertakings under the Greek Insurance Regulation
Law.

Solvency II amendments

On 22 September 2021, the European Commission published a legislative proposal to amend the
Solvency II Directive in relation to, among other things, capital requirements, valuation of insurance
liabilities, cross-border supervision, and clarifications to the proportionality principle. The final text of
the amended Solvency II Directive was adopted by the Council on 5 November 2024 and published in
the EU's Official Journal on 8 January 2025 as Directive (EU) 2025/2. Member States must implement
the Directive into national law by 29 January 2027. In addition, the IRRD was published on the same
date, also requiring transposition into national law by 29 January 2027.

EU Insurance Recovery and Resolution Directive (IRRD)

The IRRD shifts the regulatory philosophy from ex-post management of insurer failure to ex-ante
management of financial distress. It requires insurers representing at least 60 per cent. of the respective
insurance market to engage in forward-looking recovery planning and submit pre-emptive recovery
plans to national supervisory authorities. Member States must establish national insurance resolution
authorities, either within existing authorities or as new self-standing legal entities, ensuring effective
cross-border cooperation, with EIOPA having a coordinating role. Resolution authorities are equipped
with resolution tools and procedures, including write-down and conversion of capital instruments, debt
instruments and other eligible liabilities (applying first to equity instruments and Tier 1 instruments,
then to Tier 2 instruments (such as the Notes) and then to other instruments with a higher ranking in
liquidation), solvent run-offs, portfolio transfers and, in limited cases, bridge institutions, to ensure
continuity of cover and policyholder protection without defaulting to liquidation. Certain liabilities are
excluded from write-down and conversion tools to avoid adverse outcomes for policyholders. Normal
insolvency proceedings remain the alternative path for insurers that cannot be resolved, and the IRRD
provides for a no-creditor-worse-off principle (i.e. that no creditor should be in a worse position through
use of the tools provided under the IRRD than it would have been in the case of the insolvency of the
relevant insurer).

Insurance Distribution Directive

The Insurance Distribution Directive has been transposed into Greek law by Greek Law 4583/2018, as
amended, which regulates the distribution of insurance products by insurance intermediaries (such as
the subsidiaries of the Issuer) and insurance undertakings when acting as insurance distributors.
Compliance with Greek Law 4583/2018 is supervised by the BoG. The framework requires insurers to
comply, among others, with information and disclosure requirements (including disclosure



                                                   - 137 -

requirements regarding remuneration, obliging insurers to disclose to their customers the nature of
remuneration they receive) and certain conduct of business rules (including a general obligation to act
honestly, fairly and professionally in accordance with customers' best interests). It also requires
insurance distributors to establish and maintain appropriate policies and procedures for the approval,
review and distribution of insurance products in accordance with the product oversight and governance
requirements and the identified target market. In addition, the Insurance Distribution Directive sets out
requirements relating to the remuneration of sales staff and conflicts of interest and introduces a
mandatory product oversight and governance process for assessing the suitability of insurance products
for customers. Greek Law 4583/2018 also establishes professional knowledge and competence
requirements, including ongoing professional training obligations, for insurance distributors.

Consumer protection

In addition to the prudential supervision exercised by the BoG, certain consumer-protection authorities
may have jurisdiction where an insurance undertaking deals with policyholders acting in their capacity
as consumers. In particular, the Consumers' Ombudsman and the General Secretariat for Consumer
Protection may exercise supervisory or enforcement powers within their respective fields of
competence, with a view to safeguarding consumer rights, including in relation to transparency, the
fairness of contractual terms and compliance with applicable consumer-protection legislation. The
general consumer protection framework under Greek Law 2251/1994, as amended, also applies to
insurance products offered to consumers, including the rules on unfair commercial practices and unfair
terms in consumer contracts.

Insurance contracts are principally governed by Greek Law 2496/1997, which sets minimum standards
governing the rights of insurers and insured parties, the content of insurance contracts, the pre-
contractual and ongoing disclosure obligations of each party, the applicable timeframes and the rights
to cancel or rescind. Greek Law 2496/1997 also contains mandatory provisions designed to protect
policyholders, particularly in relation to pre-contractual disclosure, the insurer's duty to inform, the
consequences of non-disclosure or misrepresentation, premium payment, termination of insurance
contracts and claims handling.

Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA)

Since 17 January 2025, insurance undertakings must comply with DORA, which establishes a directly
applicable EU framework for digital operational resilience across the financial sector. DORA imposes
requirements in relation to ICT risk management, incident handling and reporting, digital resilience
testing, and ICT third-party risk management. DORA complements the existing outsourcing framework
under the Greek Insurance Regulation Law in respect of critical or important functions, as well as cloud
outsourcing requirements under BoG Executive Committee Act No. 180/3/17.12.2020, which adopted
the EIOPA Guidelines on outsourcing to cloud service providers (EIOPA-BoS-20/002). Compliance
with DORA by Greek insurance undertakings is subject to the supervisory oversight of the Bank of
Greece.

Anti‑Money Laundering and Counter‑Terrorist Financing (AML/CFT)

The principal national legislation is Greek Law 4557/2018 (the "Greek AML Law"), which transposed
Directive (EU) 2015/849 and was subsequently amended to transpose Directive (EU) 2018/843 and
Directive (EU) 2018/1673. The Greek AML Law designates insurance undertakings and insurance
intermediaries as obliged entities, requiring them to implement, appropriate internal policies, controls
and procedures, conduct institution-wide risk assessments, risk‑based customer due diligence
(including identification of beneficial owners and beneficiaries prior to claims payment, where
applicable), enhanced due diligence for higher‑risk relationships, ongoing monitoring, record‑keeping
and suspicious transaction reporting to the competent anti-money laundering authority, while remaining
subject to applicable supervisory oversight by the BoG.

AI Act

The Issuer may be subject to the AI Act to the extent it deploys artificial intelligence systems. The AI

risk AI systems under Article 6(2) and Annex III of the AI Act. Such classification may apply to AI
systems used by the Issuer in underwriting, risk assessment or claims processing. Deployers of high-
risk AI systems are subject to obligations under the AI Act relating to human oversight, transparency
towards affected persons, data quality, risk management, conformity assessment, record-keeping and
registration in the EU database. The obligations applicable to high-risk AI systems under the AI Act
have applied since 2 August 2026 (with some exceptions where a later compliance date applies, such
as certain AI systems which are components of the large-scale IT systems as described in Article 111(1)
of the AI Act).
